We’re betting our $5.5M seed round that the next leap in AI coding won’t come from OpenAI or Anthropic.

Beacon continuously distills your sessions into reusable skills across Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and 20+ harnesses, so your next agent can learn from the last.

Yann LeCun was right & nobody in this industry wants to say it out loud.



109 million parameters beat 72 billion.



He has spent years saying scale is not the thing that makes a model understand the world. Meta bet the other way. He left in November and started his own lab in Paris.



Last Thursday he published the proof.



The theory everyone has been running on since 2024 is that if you train models big enough, on text, on images, on sound, they all end up with the same picture of reality inside them. Size does it. Nobody ever proved that part.



Randall Balestriero and LeCun proved it. And the proof says size was never doing the work.



What does the work is which two things you show a model together.



A photo and the caption of that photo are two views of one thing. Models trained on pairs like that get there fast.



Two paragraphs pulled from the same document are not two views of one thing. Models trained on those get there slowly and expensively.



Next word prediction is the second kind. That is what every chatbot in the world runs on.



In their tests the first method reached the same understanding after 21.6 million examples. Next word prediction needed 900 million.



And a 109 million parameter text model ended up closer to an image model's view of the world than a 72 billion parameter language model was.



660 times smaller.

I'm now building an "improvements" feature into all of my personal vibecoded applications: a freeform text input that's hooked up to an agent that yolo implements whatever is submitted.



It's an interesting experience -- the activation energy barrier to sanding any rough edge or implementing any new feature becomes extremely low. Someone else who uses one of the applications I created has already implemented 150 improvements over the course of a few days. This pattern feels like a new kind of tool -- liquid software? -- and every application that doesn't have this feature now has a slightly rigid and anachronistic flavor. Why can't I just tell it how I want it to be different?



Now, it's not obvious to me how this pattern can or should scale. Does it become unmaintainable after a while? (Maybe model intelligence improvement outstrips my feature appetite such that it's fine?) How does collaborative software work in this model? Can software designed this way be secure and reliable?



Whatever the larger questions about broader deployment, it definitely works great in a personal context. It reminds me a little of the visions of Lisp/Lisp machines, Smalltalk, and HyperCard -- systems that the user can take control of and modify. Those visions never quite worked, though: the vast majority of software today is not end-user modifiable in any useful way. So, while this "liquid" affordance is a very small touch, the way it changes one's relation to the software feels a bit transgressive and empowering in a Lickliderian and Engelbartian way.

✅ Look for missing information and potential biases.



✅ Verify important claims against reliable sources.



Most importantly, don't confuse a confident AI response with an unbiased or accurate one.



AI should help us think more critically, not replace our critical thinking. 🚀

Incidents and security

- Oct 27: GPT-6.1 Sol was degraded for about 78 minutes, then resolved.

- Don't run Codex inside ~/Downloads (Forever Security found a planted AGENTS.md), and don't install it from reseller one-liners (Symantec caught one turning the sandbox off).

As the agent economy grows, trust mechanisms will matter just as much as the intelligence of the agents themselves. Reliable identity, meaningful performance history, and verifiable delivery can help create stronger foundations for agent-to-agent commerce.

All of us understand that useful software is getting easier to create. But generating code, completing end-to-end engineering work, and creating business value are moving at very different rates. 



Digging into this from different angles. Epoch, for example, estimates that a fixed level of AI performance is getting cheaper 13x per year for the past 4 years. That's across math, science, and game projects. 



Anthropic's 100k C compiler experiment is well known: 20k API spend, roughly $200 per kLOC of code, but the compiler had major limitations, lots of bugs, and wasn't really comparable to a fully functional C compiler. 



An early 2026 Microsoft study estimates 25% more merged pull requests. Anthropic has shared bigger stats with us. What's not clear, though, is whether this translated into business value. It's an observational study, and in general, I am skeptical of observational data about increased activity.



A more recent September 2026 paper has impressive stats: 240%+ more commits, 80% more projects, 30% more releases, but it's output gains, not cost reductions. 



It's clear that cheaper software creation is going to make previously uneconomical software worth building: bespoke tools, small markets. I built a bunch of app & skills I would never have bothered to write actual code for before, for example. why? because it's cheap and easy.



Estimating value for these can be tricky. If, for example, somebody never created a piece of software that could create 10k of value because software costs 50k to create, and all of a sudden that 50k became 1k, the total economic value that's created is 9k, not 49k. This kind of "more is more" can be tricky to measure in terms of actual gain, either for a company or for society. 



The one other thing that people don't seem to keep in mind is that AI created software (all software?) comes with a poison pill: catastrophic bugs. 



If our ability to create new software grows out of proportion with our ability to detect them or, worse, fix them, we end up in a crisis-driven world. 



The world of crypto offers a warning here: there's a mind-numbing repetition of bugs with massive impact. Think about that. Would you tolerate that from your bank? 



Thinking about this as well as value capture from other world-changing inventions. Comment with ideas and thoughts.

Only about a quarter of human diseases have an approved therapy. By some estimates it's a few percent. Most of those treatments slow a disease rather than stop it.



Closing that gap is what the AI-cures-everything story promises. Build a system smart enough and the cures hidden in what we already know will fall out. I have worked at the intersection of machine learning and biology for three decades, and I believe #AI will eventually transform human health. The capabilities arriving now are extraordinary. But the promise rests on an assumption that is simply false: that we already understand human biology well enough for a clever enough reasoner to find the answers in it. We don't.



More than 90% of drugs entering clinical trials fail, a number that has barely moved in decades. In the large majority of those failures the molecule was engineered just fine. The mechanism it targeted was wrong. We are doing a pretty good job at manufacturing keys, but they are generally for the wrong locks. And because nobody wants to fail in the clinic, the industry has retreated to the locks it already trusts: 38 targets now have more than 50 programs against each of them, while the number of novel targets advanced per year fell from roughly 100 in 2015 to about 30 in 2024.



AI will not reason its way past this. Biology wasn't engineered. It is the product of billions of years of messy, stochastic evolution, and the variation that produced is too vast and too idiosyncratic to work out in the abstract. You have to measure it. Aimed at a biology this thinly sampled, AI will mostly help us generate failures faster.



I founded @insitro because getting to the right locks requires a different kind of system. We generate multimodal human and cellular data at scale, use machine learning to find causal drivers of disease, and test those hypotheses experimentally. Virtual Human™ is built for causal discovery; TherML™ turns what it finds into the right therapeutic intervention. It is working: first-in-class programs internally and with partners, three #ALS targets that Virtual Human™ identified and @bmsnews nominated, and additional collaborations with @EliLillyandCo and @GileadSciences .



Today we are launching Deep Phenotype: Scaled Biology, Deep Causality. Issue one is "Drug Discovery Has No Magic Wands," the first half of a two-part essay on the magical thinking currently running through our field and what I think it will actually take. After that you will hear from insitro's own scientists and engineers, people who work across computation and experiment because the problem requires both.



Getting this right is hard, and we do not have all of it worked out. I hope you will follow along and think it through with us.

Inspired by the spinor nature of spin–orbit-coupled electronic states, we introduce eSpinor, an SU(2)-equivariant graph neural network that propagates spinor features to predict spin-orbit coupling (SOC)-dependent magnetic properties.



Magnetic properties such as magnetic anisotropy, excitation energies, and spin dynamics guide the design of single-molecule magnets, MRI probes, and other spin-based technologies. Predicting them often requires CASSCF-SO calculations to capture multireference electronic structure, which can take hours for a single molecular geometry.



SO(3)-equivariance has improved the accuracy of rotation-invariant energy predictions in machine-learning interatomic potentials. Can we take this idea further by imposing SU(2)-equivariance on spinor features as an inductive bias for predicting magnetic properties?



Our main contributions are:

(1) SU(2)-equivariant spinor message passing: Hamiltonian-derived spinors and classified interaction types enable gauge-covariant updates and gauge-invariant predictions

(3) Spin dynamics and solvent transfer: More accurate predictions for a dysprosium MRI probe, with benefits extending from water to methanol without retraining



Our results support SU(2)-equivariant spinor message passing as a useful inductive bias for molecular magnetism, even when the targets are integer-rank tensors or invariant scalars.



With this framework, we’re excited to help accelerate the discovery of new magnetic molecules and deepen our understanding of their spin dynamics!

System Design: How would you build an AI agent orchestration platform?



Imagine asking 3 AI agents to complete one task:



→ Agent 1 writes the code.

→ Agent 2 reviews it.

→ Agent 3 runs tests before merging.



Sounds simple, right? 



The real challenge is coordinating everything reliably.



1. Orchestration Layer



- A central orchestrator assigns tasks, tracks workflow state, and coordinates agents.



2. Workflow Engine



- Represent dependencies as a DAG. 

- Code writing must finish before review starts, and tests run after approval. 

- Independent tasks can execute in parallel.



Each task follows a state machine:



"PENDING → READY → RUNNING → COMPLETED"



On failure:



"RUNNING → RETRY_WAIT → READY"



If retries are exhausted, the task moves to "FAILED".



Persist state transitions so workflows can recover after crashes. 



A task becomes "READY" only when its dependencies are satisfied.



3. Execution Queue



- Use Kafka or a durable job queue to distribute tasks to workers.

- Workers claim jobs, execute them, and report results. 

- Use idempotency keys to prevent duplicate processing.



4. Failure Handling



Failures are inevitable. Design for them.



- Transient errors: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter.

- Repeated failures: Move tasks to a dead-letter queue for investigation.

- Worker crashes: Use leases and heartbeats to detect abandoned tasks and safely reassign them.

- Model/API timeouts: Apply timeouts, retry limits, and circuit breakers.

- Partial failures: Persist completed outputs so successful agents don't need to rerun unnecessarily.

- Invalid agent output: Validate results before allowing dependent tasks to proceed.



Never assume a retry means the previous execution didn't happen. 



Use idempotency and durable checkpoints to avoid duplicate side effects.



5. Shared Context



- Store task instructions, agent outputs, code diffs, logs, and conversation history in shared storage. 

- Pass each agent only the context it needs.



6. Conflict Prevention



- Give coding agents isolated Git branches or worktrees. 

- Validate diffs, run tests, and merge only after conflict checks and required approvals.



7. Observability & Cost Control



- Track token usage, model costs, execution time, retries, and failure rates. 

- Set budgets and stop runaway workflows.



8. Pause, Resume & Cancel



Persist workflow state in PostgreSQL.



- Pause: Stop scheduling new tasks and let active workers reach safe checkpoints.

- Resume: Requeue eligible tasks.

- Cancel: Stop pending tasks and signal active workers to terminate safely.



Keep "FAILED" and "CANCELLED" separate: one means execution failed; the other means execution was intentionally stopped.



Architecture at a glance:



Developer → API → Orchestrator → Workflow Engine → Durable Queue → Agent Workers



Supporting services:



- PostgreSQL - workflow state and checkpoints

- Redis - caching and short-lived coordination

- Object storage - logs, artifacts, and code outputs

- Retry/DLQ mechanism - failed task recovery

- Observability - logs, metrics, traces, and cost tracking



The key principle: assume every component can fail, and make recovery part of the architecture.

Very excited to share GeoWind2Plan 🚀, our NeurIPS 2026 Spotlight paper, and a new interactive demo ✨!



We make high-resolution 3D wind predictions in seconds to guide energy-efficient drone planning.



Wind-aware planners often assume the wind field is already known. But simulating airflow around buildings takes hours of CFD, making it impractical for short drone missions when wind conditions change.



Our approach couples wind prediction with trajectory optimization. By rotating the city layout to align with a fixed reference wind, we turn wind-direction generalization into building-geometry generalization. A localized neural operator uses multi-directional distance features to predict 3D wind within a flight corridor. The planner then optimizes the drone’s path and speed in continuous 3D space to reduce energy use. In our simulations, the drone generally flies higher and faster in tailwinds, lower and slower in headwinds, and shifts sideways to exploit favorable local winds.



Corridor prediction takes about 3 seconds versus roughly 8 hours for full-domain CFD. Compared with wind-agnostic planning, our method reduces average energy use per kilometer by 12.7% in headwinds, 6.9% in tailwinds, and 4.5% in crosswinds in CFD-evaluated simulations. It captures 75–88% of the energy savings achieved with CFD-reference wind fields.



Moving forward, we will focus on turning AI predictions of the physical world into actionable decisions for autonomous systems. Follow our lab for updates: dual.xiongyexiao.com



Explore the demo: move the start 🚩 and goal ⛳, change the wind, and watch the airflow and routes respond.

I’m starting a new early-stage AI fund, doing what I love: partnering with founders from company formation on bold bets, long before consensus.



The fund’s LPs will include Sequoia, Jeff Dean, Sachin Katti, Philip Wong (my Stanford professor and Chief Scientist adviser to TSMC), and others whose work has shaped our industry and how I think about AI’s future.



I’ll remain a partner at Sequoia and keep serving on my boards on Sequoia’s behalf.



Sequoia has been my home for the past 11 years. I joined as the youngest investor the firm had ever hired. I grew up here. Through years of intense debate and shared work, I found lifelong mentors and friends who took me under their wing and taught me this craft. They taught me to aim high and take big swings. I’ll carry that into what I build: outsized ambition, relentless truth-seeking and curiosity, and a refusal to become complacent.



Working alongside founders has made me want to build something of my own: a firm shaped from day one around the convictions I’ve developed over the past decade.



Life has taught me not to take time for granted. This is how I want to spend mine.



Why now



We’re seeing a new way of building companies in today’s AI era. Research and products often advance together. A breakthrough can open a market or accelerate a business far faster than expected. Some companies require extraordinary capital and compute early on. Others reach meaningful scale with remarkably small teams. The rules for how big these businesses can get, and how fast, are being rewritten.



But early on, the technology is unproven, the resources required enormous, and the vision seemingly implausible.



This is what I love most: seeing the potential right from the beginning, and helping founders realize their full scale of ambition.



More than ever, it starts with an extreme willingness to believe early, with bold, independent conviction in a founder’s technical insight before any product or market validation. Then, it means helping founders take the biggest swings, giving the rare, long-term patience to see those bets through uncertainty, ambiguity, and turbulence, and serving as a level head when the stakes are highest.



I learned this kind of partnership at Sequoia. It’s the foundation of the firm I’m building.



Believing before consensus



My fascination with AI’s potential took root at Stanford in the early-to-mid 2010s, studying computer science and working in Andrew Ng’s lab. The friendships I formed connected me to a community whose people and ideas would help shape modern AI and build some of our generation’s defining companies. What stayed with me was the gap between what those people saw was possible and what the wider world could imagine.



I’m drawn to founders pursuing ambitions that sound impossible today.



I start with a simple question: “What if everything goes right?”



Then we work backward together to make it happen.



In 2023, Deepak and Abhinav set out to build a general-purpose robot brain at @SkildAI, before physical AI was a consensus bet. Their sim-to-real breakthroughs gave me conviction where earlier robotics approaches had fallen short. But the data flywheel required deployment at scale. We made commercialization as urgent as research and brought in strategic partners like NVIDIA and SoftBank to support the ambition. Three years in, Skild is advancing the frontier of physical AI with nine figures in annualized revenue.



In 2024, Ioannis and Misha founded @reflection_ai with an insight into scaling reinforcement learning. As that grew into the ambition to build a Western frontier lab for open models, the hard question was how a startup competes with labs spending tens of billions. An introduction to NVIDIA and many compute calls and recruiting events later, the team has built Beam, now one of the leading US open models.



In 2025, Anna and Azalia, the co-creators of AlphaChip, founded @RicursiveAI to design models and hardware together. From day one, we made early customers and ecosystem partners a priority. Today, they are showing order-of-magnitude improvements on real workloads, working with some of the industry’s most consequential players, and reaching a defining inflection point.



The ambition keeps growing as these companies scale.



@linear has always had a kind of magic to it. Now it’s the system a new generation of AI companies builds on, for teams and agents alike.



@tavus saw early that we’d one day talk to AI the way we talk to each other. Today, it’s building the human computing interface for a world of AI colleagues.



@Mach_Industries began as hydrogen experiments in an MIT dorm room. It has since become one of the most exciting next-generation defense companies.



Making the ambition possible



Being a first believer is only the beginning. Compute falls through. A deep-pocketed incumbent makes your mission its top priority. A breakthrough changes the opportunity and the capital required overnight.



These are stomach-churning moments, and early belief carries a responsibility to help make the bet work.



This is the partnership I love: turning the full ambition into concrete steps. Raising capital, securing compute and strategic partners, recruiting exceptional people, and winning the first customers together. Thinking several moves ahead while solving what’s in front of us. And as breakthroughs open new possibilities, helping founders dream even bigger.



Thank you



To the founders I’ve worked with: thank you for trusting me and Sequoia to be your first partner and first believer. It’s been the joy of a lifetime, and I can’t wait to keep building together.



Thank you to Alfred and Pat for your leadership of Sequoia and your support of my next chapter. To Roelof, for bringing me into Sequoia and believing in me from the beginning. Alfred and Roelof, you have been mentors in investing and in life. So much of what I know, and the investor I’ve become, comes from your guidance and generosity over the years. To Bill, for the close partnership and wealth of knowledge, always wrapped in humility. To Shaun, for showing me how to think deeply and imaginatively. To Michael Moritz, for inspiring 22-year-old me to dream big. To Doug, for teaching me to keep things simple. To Bogie and Jess, for bringing joy to the everyday and perspective on what matters. And to all my Sequoia teammates, for the friendship, camaraderie, and lessons I’ll carry with me.



To my family, especially my husband and my brother, who have each started companies of their own: thank you for giving me the courage to take this leap.
